text.title: Activation Framework Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Activation Framework application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The spec MUST name exactly one activation event, written as a tracked product event name plus a time window from signup (e.g. `project_created` within 7 days). Phrases such as "user is engaged", "sees value" or a list of several events are not an activation event and MUST be rejected.

rationale.source: Sean Ellis and Morgan Brown, Hacking Growth (2017), chapter on the aha moment; Facebook's '7 friends in 10 days' as reported by Chamath Palihapitiya

rule.rationale: A definition without an event name cannot be queried, so every downstream number (baseline, funnel, experiment lift) is computed against a different reading of "activated". The window matters as much as the event: `project_created` at day 60 says nothing about onboarding.

rule.statement: The chosen event MUST be backed by a comparison table showing D30 retention for users who performed the candidate event inside the window versus users who did not, with both rates and both group sizes, on at least one closed signup cohort. A candidate whose retained group is not materially larger than the non-retained group MUST NOT be selected. The table MUST carry the note that the relationship is correlational.

rationale.source: Amplitude, 'Mastering Retention' playbook; Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz, Lean Analytics (2013)

rule.rationale: Teams routinely pick the event that is easiest to push users into rather than the one that predicts retention, then celebrate a rising activation rate while D30 stays flat. Recording both rates and sizes lets a reviewer see a 5-user "lift" for what it is, and the correlational note stops the spec from promising that forcing the event will create retention.

rule.statement: The spec MUST state a baseline activation rate computed per signup-week cohort for at least four consecutive closed cohorts before any experiment is listed. A cohort is closed only when signup date plus the activation window is earlier than the data cutoff; open cohorts MUST NOT be included in the baseline.

rationale.source: Lean Analytics (Croll and Yoskovitz), cohort analysis; widely established growth-analytics practice

rule.rationale: One week of data is noise, and an open cohort under-reports activation because its users have not had the full window yet. Both errors produce a baseline that a later experiment "beats" without changing anything.

rule.statement: Every funnel step between signup and the activation event MUST be mapped to a named tracked event. A step with no event MUST be listed as `uninstrumented` with an instrumentation task, and no conversion or drop-off figure may be reported for it.

rationale.source: Hacking Growth (Ellis and Brown), instrumenting the funnel; Amplitude and Mixpanel funnel documentation

rule.rationale: Funnel maps drawn from the UI rather than from events invent steps that no query can measure, and the drop-off "found" at those steps is guesswork that the experiment backlog then optimises against.

rule.statement: Drop-off priorities MUST be ranked by absolute users lost per step (users entering the step minus users completing it) over the baseline cohorts, with the relative drop shown alongside. Ranking by percentage alone is not permitted.

rationale.source: widely established funnel-analysis practice; Lean Analytics (Croll and Yoskovitz)

rule.rationale: A 60 percent drop on a step 40 users reach loses 24 users; a 15 percent drop on a step 2,000 users reach loses 300. Percentage ranking sends the team to fix the smaller problem first.

rule.statement: Every experiment in the backlog MUST carry Impact, Confidence and Ease as integers from 1 to 10 and an ICE score equal to their arithmetic mean rounded to two decimals, exactly as computed by `templates/ice.py`. The backlog MUST be sorted by ICE descending.

rationale.source: Sean Ellis, GrowthHackers ICE prioritisation; Hacking Growth (Ellis and Brown)

rule.rationale: Mixed scales (one experiment scored 1-5, another 1-10) and ad-hoc weighting make the ranking unreproducible, so the backlog order becomes whoever argued loudest. A single formula in a script makes the order checkable.

rule.statement: Each experiment MUST name the funnel step it targets, a one-sentence hypothesis, the primary metric (activation rate within the window, or the targeted step's conversion), the current baseline value, and the minimum lift at which it ships. An experiment missing any of these MUST NOT enter the backlog.

rationale.source: Hacking Growth (Ellis and Brown); widely established A/B testing practice

rule.rationale: Without a pre-declared ship threshold, every result gets rationalised after the fact and the "winning" changes accumulate with zero net effect on activation. Tying each experiment to a step keeps the backlog aligned with the drop-off ranking instead of with feature wishes.

rule.statement: The weekly activation dashboard specified MUST report activation rate per signup-week cohort, only for closed cohorts, segmented by acquisition channel, and MUST show the same window as the activation event definition. Changing the event or window MUST produce a new dashboard series, never an in-place edit of history.

rationale.source: widely established cohort-reporting practice; Amplitude retention documentation

rule.rationale: Mixing a 7-day and a 14-day window on one chart, or plotting last week's cohort at day 3, produces the dip at the right edge that teams misread as a regression every single week.
